mcqs.question: In a feed system with a 50:1 ratio of feed reads to post writes, which should the architecture optimize first?
options: Read latency and read cost, since reads happen far more often than writes
Write latency, since publishing is the rarer and thus more important operation
Storage cost, since it dominates regardless of the read/write ratio
Neither — reads and writes should always get equal engineering priority
mcqs.explanation: When reads outnumber writes 50:1, the aggregate cost of the read path dominates total system cost even if each individual write is more complex. Optimizing writes first would improve the rarer operation at the expense of the one users hit constantly. Storage matters but doesn't override the read/write skew, and treating both as equal priority ignores the actual traffic shape.

mcqs.question: Why does pure fan-out-on-write break down for a celebrity account with 50M followers?
options: It doesn't — fan-out-on-write scales identically regardless of follower count
One publish turns into tens of millions of individual writes, creating a write storm that can delay fan-out for everyone else queued behind it
The post itself becomes too large to store once it has that many followers
Celebrity accounts are technically forbidden from using fan-out-on-write by the API
mcqs.explanation: Fan-out-on-write cost scales with follower count, so a 50M-follower account turns one post into 50M writes — a storm that can back up the shared fan-out queue and delay other users' posts. There's no such API restriction, and post size is unrelated to follower count; the whole point of this slide is that the strategy does NOT scale identically at the tail.

mcqs.question: Why is a hybrid fan-out strategy usually worth its added complexity over a single pure strategy?
options: It's simpler to implement than either pure strategy alone
It removes the need for any ranking step later in the pipeline
Real follower-count distributions are heavy-tailed, so a single strategy that's efficient for typical accounts fails at the celebrity tail, and vice versa
It eliminates the need for asynchronous fan-out workers entirely
mcqs.explanation: The hybrid exists specifically because follower counts are heavy-tailed: push is efficient for typical accounts but breaks at the celebrity tail, and pull handles the tail but is expensive for everyone if applied universally. It's genuinely more complex to implement, not simpler, doesn't remove ranking, and still needs async workers for the push side.

mcqs.question: A team proposes computing every user's feed fresh, by joining across all their followees' posts, on every single feed load. What's the core flaw?
options: Nothing — this is exactly how production feed systems like Twitter work
It would violate the functional requirement that feeds be ordered chronologically
Joins across followees are impossible to express in any database query language
It applies the expensive fan-in-on-read pattern to the entire read-dominated traffic, instead of reserving it for the narrow celebrity-follow case where precomputing would be worse
mcqs.explanation: Since reads vastly outnumber writes, making every read do the expensive join means paying the most expensive operation on the highest-volume path — the opposite of the hybrid's targeted approach, which reserves live merging for the small slice of celebrity followees. The join is expressible in SQL; ordering isn't the issue at all.
